metadata.title: Digital inequality in Austria: Empirical evidence from the survey of the OECD “Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies”

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the OECD PIAAC 2011/2012 survey for Austria and restricts the analytic sample to employed and self-employed respondents who passed the ICT core stage and took the PSTRE (digital problem-solving) assessment. The authors state that all data work and estimation were conducted in R using the svyPV package, which is designed to account for plausible values and survey weights in complex test survey designs; however, the manuscript does not report the specific weight variable name(s). For the PSTRE regression, the dependent variable is a PSTRE score on a 0–500 scale and the authors explicitly use a PV-aware workflow (svyPV), implying appropriate handling of the complex survey structure. For the Eurostat time-series descriptive analyses (2012–2019), the paper does not describe applying survey weights or replicate weights, so weighting strategy for those components is not documented in the provided text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports using the svyPV package to conduct calculations that take into account plausible values and survey weights, but it does not document how missing data in covariates or outcomes were handled (e.g., complete-case vs imputation). This is a reporting gap because missingness can affect regression estimates and subgroup comparisons, especially when restricting to employed/self-employed and ICT-proficient respondents. The authors do describe exclusions related to ICT core stage and PSTRE participation, but they do not specify a missing-data rule for the regression variables.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses Austrian PIAAC 2011/2012 microdata. Starts from 5130 participants aged 16–65 in Austria, then restricts to respondents with proven ICT knowledge who took the PSTRE (digital problem-solving in technology-rich environments) assessment (excluding those who never used a computer, failed the ICT core stage, or refused PSTRE). Further restricts the sample to employed and self-employed respondents, yielding 2542 observations (1303 men, 1239 women). For the regression analysis, independent variables include books at home at age 16 (5-level categorical), gender, age (centered), test language (native vs non-native), years of schooling (centered), urbanisation (rescaled to 0–1), and an ICT use index in everyday life (Warm’s WLE quintiles).

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011/2012 Austria (employed/self-employed, PSTRE digital problem solving)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression with PV-aware estimation (svyPV). Reported coefficient estimates and statistical significance (no ML metrics such as RMSE/R²/AUC). Key reported effects: Female −7.36 points (Model 1, p<0.01); Female −13.86 points (Model 2, p<0.05); Age −0.69 to −0.80 per year (p<0.01); Years of schooling +3.89 or +3.24 per year (p<0.01/p<0.05); ICT use index +6.20 (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011/2012 Austria data (employed/self-employed respondents who completed PSTRE), the study leveraged Gender, Books at home (age 16), Age, Years of schooling, and ICT use in everyday life to model PSTRE digital problem-solving score, finding that women score lower on average and that higher socio-economic background is associated with higher PSTRE scores, with the gender effect becoming statistically insignificant once ICT use in everyday life is included. This indicates that policies aiming to reduce digital inequality should prioritize increasing everyday ICT engagement among disadvantaged groups, because observed gender and socio-economic gaps in digital problem solving appear partly mediated by ICT familiarity rather than reflecting fixed differences alone.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes Austria’s PIAAC 2011/2012 survey, focusing on the PSTRE (digital problem-solving in technology-rich environments) cognitive domain for employed and self-employed adults who passed the ICT core stage and completed PSTRE. The analytic sample comprises 2542 respondents from Austria. Using PV-aware estimation in R (svyPV), the authors estimate stepwise OLS regressions where Gender and Books at home (age 16) are central predictors, alongside Age, Years of schooling, test language, urbanisation, and an ICT use index in everyday life. Results show women’s PSTRE scores are lower (e.g., −7.36 points in Model 1, p<0.01), socio-economic background is positively related to PSTRE (significant for higher book categories), and Age is negatively associated while Years of schooling is positively associated. When ICT use in everyday life is added, gender becomes statistically insignificant and only the top socio-economic category remains significant, suggesting ICT engagement is closely linked to PSTRE performance; however, causality cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional regression and missing-data handling is not fully documented.
